title: Week 2 · Multi-Step Equations and Literal Formulas

lessons.title: Week 2 · Day 2 · Solving Literal Equations and Interpreting Units
lessons.body:
ALGEBRA I • UNIT 1 • WEEK 2 • DAY 2 OF 5 • 55 MINUTES
Essential question: How do we rearrange a formula to express a different quantity, and when is that rearrangement valid?
Learning targets: Isolate a named variable in a multi-letter equation, explain denominator restrictions, check formulas in context, and interpret units. Standards: A-CED.4 and N-Q.1. Prerequisites: equivalent equations, fractional operations, and units of measurement.

LAUNCH (5 min)
A walking club travels d = 12 miles at a constant rate r = 3 miles per hour. Find its travel time t without guessing. Now imagine you know only d and r, not their numerical values. What expression would represent t? Compare the statement t = 4 hours, which describes one trip, with t = d/r, which describes a relationship among many possible trips. Explain why you must not divide by a rate of zero. Name the units of every quantity in your explanation.

EXPLICIT INSTRUCTION (12 min)
A literal equation is an equation containing multiple letters that stand for quantities. Solving a literal equation for a named variable means using equality-preserving operations to express that variable in terms of the others. Treat other letters as known quantities, even though their numerical values may be unknown. The resulting formula can apply to many situations. Always record restrictions that prevent division by zero; in applied settings, also interpret permitted values and units.

WORKED MODEL 1: Distance = rate × time. Begin with d = rt and isolate t. Divide both sides by r to obtain t = d/r, provided r ≠ 0. If d = 150 km and r = 50 km/hour, then t = 3 hours, since 150 km ÷ (50 km/hour) = 3 hours. Check the original: 50 km/hour × 3 hours = 150 km. When r = 0, division is not permitted. If d ≠ 0, there is no value of t that satisfies d = 0t; if d = 0, every real t satisfies the algebraic equation, although context may narrow the possible times.

WORKED MODEL 2: Rectangle perimeter P = 2l + 2w. To isolate width w, subtract 2l from both sides: P − 2l = 2w. Divide by 2: w = (P − 2l)/2 = P/2 − l. For P = 40 cm and l = 13 cm, width w = 7 cm. Check: 2(13 cm) + 2(7 cm) = 40 cm. Algebraically division by 2 is always legal; a real rectangle also needs l > 0 and w > 0, which requires P > 2l.

WORKED MODEL 3: Fahrenheit F = (9/5)C + 32. Isolate Celsius C. Subtract 32 on both sides: F − 32 = (9/5)C. Multiply by 5/9: C = (5/9)(F − 32). At F = 68°F, C = 20°C. Check: (9/5)(20) + 32 = 68. Note that the offset 32 must be removed before scaling.

GENERAL METHOD: (1) Circle the desired variable. (2) Name the operations to undo, in reverse order. (3) Perform each operation on both sides. (4) Write nonzero restrictions and any contextual limits. (5) Substitute a numerical example into the ORIGINAL equation to verify.

GUIDED PRACTICE (12 min)
Write a formula first, then use the provided values. Show every operation on both sides and indicate the restriction for division.
A. A rectangle has area A = lw. Isolate w. Then use A = 84 cm² and l = 12 cm to determine w in centimeters. Explain how the area units simplify.
B. From y = mx + b, solve for x. Then use y = 17, m = 3, and b = 5 to find x. State the condition on m. Explain the special case when m = 0.
C. Electrical energy E equals power P times time t: E = Pt. Isolate t. If E = 360 joules and P = 60 watts (joules/second), interpret your answer in seconds.
After each problem, check by substitution into the given original formula. A valid answer includes both symbolic reasoning and the physical units when relevant.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE (16 min)
Show equivalent equations, give each necessary nonzero restriction, and verify the numerical result by substitution.
1. Solve A = lw for w. A rectangular garden has A = 96 m² and l = 12 m; find w and report units.
2. Solve P = 2l + 2w for l. A rectangle has P = 54 cm and w = 11 cm; find l.
3. Solve y = mx + b for m. Use y = 29, b = 5, x = 6. What happens to the algebraic relationship if x = 0?
4. Solve V = lwh for h. A storage box has V = 180 cm³, l = 9 cm, and w = 5 cm. Find h and identify conditions on l and w for division.
5. Rearrange F = (9/5)C + 32 to express C in terms of F. Find C when F = 77°F and check with the original formula.
6. A triangle has area A = (1/2)bh. Solve for b and state a restriction. If A = 30 m² and h = 5 m, find the base in meters.
7. ERROR ANALYSIS: A student claims that from y = mx + b it follows that x = y/m − b. Test the claim with y = 14, m = 2, and b = 4. Identify the incorrect step and write the correct general formula. Why do parentheses matter?
8. EXTENSION: Write a realistic situation described by F = B + nr, where F and B are amounts of money, n counts services, and r is the charge per service. Solve for r, state when this formula is defined, and interpret its units.

Choose at least three problems from different contexts for full written explanations. Practice does not create a grade solely because a lesson was opened or marked complete.

EXIT TICKET (10 min)
On your own, solve the circumference formula C = 2πr for radius r. State why division is allowed, and name the unit of r if C is measured in centimeters. Then find the radius when C = 10π cm and verify by substituting into the ORIGINAL circumference equation. In one sentence, explain the difference between a formula for r and a numerical value of r. Submit all steps as evidence for teacher feedback.

SELF-CHECK AND SUPPORT
Before submitting, check that you have isolated the requested letter, not merely replaced it with a number; applied each operation to both sides; used parentheses around grouped expressions such as (y − b); recorded restrictions for denominators; and checked the original formula rather than only the transformed version. For visual access, write fractions with a horizontal bar or as carefully grouped parenthesized expressions. Read units aloud during dimensional checks, e.g., square meters divided by meters gives meters. If stuck, begin with d = rt: what operation reverses multiplication by r? Never cancel a letter without first checking whether it could be zero.
learningTargets: I can solve a literal equation for a specified variable by preserving equality.
I can identify nonzero denominator restrictions and explain exceptional cases.
I can check a rearranged formula with real numerical values and interpret measurement units.
